content: Polygonatum, commonly known as King Solomon's Seal or Solomon's Seal, is a genus comprising approximately 50 species of flowering plants. These plants belong to the family Ruscaceae, though they were previously classified under the lily family, Liliaceae. Certain species within this genus possess medicinal properties. For instance, Polygonatum sibiricum is widely used in traditional Chinese medicine as a tisane, referred to as Duong Gul Le in Korea. Additionally, some shoots of Polygonatum are edible and can be prepared similarly to asparagus. The roots, after undergoing proper treatment, are also consumable and serve as a rich source of starch. The medicinal applications of Solomon's Seal primarily involve its root. Traditionally, the root has been employed to address a variety of conditions, ranging from menopausal symptoms to the treatment of broken bones. When applied topically, the root is believed to accelerate the healing process of cuts, bruises, skin irritations, and inflammations. It is also used as a facial wash to treat acne, blemishes, and other skin imperfections. When consumed as a tea, Solomon's Seal is said to alleviate numerous symptoms, including those associated with menopause, indigestion, diabetes, broken bones, insomnia, kidney pain, and even infertility. Its potential role in managing diabetes was first documented in 1930 by Langecker, who observed its effectiveness in combating nutritional hyperglycemia. However, it was noted that it did not counteract hyperglycemia caused by adrenaline release. This effect is thought to be due to the plant's glucokinin content.
